t: 3759. Count Elements With at Least K Greater Values
o: An element qualifies when at least k other elements are strictly greater than it. In [3,1,2] with k=1, both 1 and 2 qualify (answer 2); in [5,5,5] with k=2 nobody does. Sorting reveals a one-line criterion: the k-th largest value t = sorted[n-k] is the smallest value that does NOT qualify, because exactly the values strictly below t have at least k elements above them. So the answer is the count of elements strictly less than t (and all n elements when k = 0).
k: #elements strictly greater than v >= k is equivalent to v < (k-th largest element).
Sorting once and taking sorted[n-k] as the threshold reduces the problem to a counting query.
Duplicates are handled automatically since the comparison is strict.

a.i: Sort ascending; let t be the k-th largest. Every element strictly smaller than t has at least k strictly greater elements; every element >= t has fewer. Count elements < t with a binary search (or a linear scan over the sorted array).
s: Sort a copy of nums ascending; set t = a[n-k].
Return the number of elements strictly less than t (bisect_left position of t).
a.t: O(n log n) - sorting dominates; the threshold lookup and count are linear/logarithmic

w: Derive the threshold criterion on the whiteboard - it makes the duplicate handling obvious. Pitfalls: using >= instead of strict inequality at the threshold, mishandling k = 0, and confusing 'k-th largest' indexing (a[n-k] in an ascending array). Follow-up: solve in expected O(n) with quickselect, or count elements with at least k strictly smaller values.
